title: Your Move: Escape the City Before It Falls

beats.text: The last helicopter out of the city lifts off in ten seconds.
And five hundred dead are between you and it.
Below you, the whole city is burning. And you are one jump from getting out.
Twenty four hours ago, you were asleep. Every choice from here is your move. Get them right, and you live.
Here's how this works. Every chapter, you get one choice. Pause the video, pick your move, and keep count. At the end, we'll see if you made it.
Six A.M. Every phone in the city screams at once.
You run to the window. Down on the street, people are running. And some of the people chasing them are not people anymore.
On the news, a reporter is mid sentence when something pulls her off camera.
Across the street, a building is on fire. Then your power cuts out.
And someone is pounding on your door. Not knocking. Pounding.
You've got about ten seconds to think. So you think about what matters. Water. Food. A way out.
The door frame cracks.
Your move. Barricade the door? Or grab your bag and run, right now?
If you barricaded, you're safe. For an hour. Then the smoke from across the street fills your floor.
You crawl to the window to breathe. Twelve floors up. No way down. And the door is still blocked by everything you own.
Most people who die in fires never touch a flame. It's the smoke that gets them.

paper.title: FIRE FACT
paper.src: smoke inhalation causes the majority of fire deaths (U.S. fire safety data)

beats.text: If you ran, good move. You open the door just as your neighbor lunges. He's already turned.
He flies past you, into your apartment. You slam the door behind him.
You grab the bag you packed for camping last summer. Water bottle. Flashlight. Knife. First aid kit.
Rule one of any emergency. Don't wait for someone to tell you to leave.

paper.title: RULE ONE
paper.src: evacuation guidance: leave early, before routes are blocked

beats.text: The hallway lights are flashing red. Fire alarm. And somewhere below you, someone is screaming.
Your building has twelve floors. And the elevator still works.
Your move. The elevator? Or the stairs?
If you took the elevator, it stops between floors four and five. Then the doors start to open. From the outside.
Grey fingers slide through the gap. Then a face. Then another. You're in a steel box, and they're opening it.
In an emergency, never take the elevator. When the power goes, it becomes a steel box with no way out.

paper.title: EMERGENCY RULE
paper.src: standard fire and emergency evacuation guidance

beats.text: If you took the stairs, good move. But ten floors down, the dead are already coming up.
So you do what you did as a kid. You slide down the railing, straight over their heads.
Your hands burn. Your bag almost rips off your back. But you're moving faster than anything on those stairs.
The lobby. And the front door is locked.
So you rip the fire extinguisher off the wall, and you swing.
You hit the lobby running, and go straight through the glass door.
Seven A.M. The highway out of the city is one giant parking lot. Ten thousand cars. Nobody's moving.
Car doors hang open. Engines still running. People left everything and ran.
Somewhere behind you, a truck horn is stuck on. Nobody is left to let go of it.
And the dead are walking between the lanes.
So you run across the roofs. Car to car to car.
Then a car alarm goes off under your feet. A hundred and twenty decibels.
Every head on the highway turns toward you.
You've got maybe forty seconds before they reach you.
Your move. Steal the motorcycle next to you? Or keep going on foot?
If you took the motorcycle, the keys aren't in it. You lose forty seconds. That's all they need.
Engines are loud. On a silent highway, an engine is a dinner bell.

paper.title: NOISE = DANGER
paper.src: in a quiet city, engine noise carries for blocks

beats.text: If you kept going on foot, good move. You drop off the side of the road, and down into the subway.
Ten seconds after you disappear down the stairs, the first of them reaches the car where you were standing.
Eight thirty. The subway is pitch black. Your flashlight is the only light underground.
Somewhere in the dark, water is dripping. And every drop sounds like footsteps.
Then your flashlight catches something on the tracks ahead. It's moving. It's a rat. Hundreds of them. All running the same way.
Then you hear it. A train. Running on its own. Nobody driving.
You press flat against the wall as it screams past, three inches from your face.
In the windows, you see faces. Pressed against the glass. Not one of them is blinking.
Down here, the rail next to the tracks carries over six hundred volts. One step on it, and it's over.

paper.title: THE THIRD RAIL
paper.src: subway third rails typically carry about 600-750 volts DC

beats.text: Then the tunnel splits.
Your move. Follow the tracks? Or follow the rats along the ledge?
beats.opt2: Follow the rats along the ledge
Follow the rats along the ledge

beats.text: If you followed the tracks, a second train comes. And there's nowhere to stand but the third rail.
Six hundred volts or a train. There's no good way out of that tunnel.
If you followed the rats, good move. Rats run from danger, and they always know the way up.
Two hundred yards later, daylight through a grate. A ladder. Up.
Ten A.M. The tunnel comes up under City Hospital.
The emergency room doors are wide open. Gurneys everywhere. Nobody behind the desk.
Your arm is cut from the glass door. Out here, one infected cut can kill you.

paper.title: WHY YOU NEED MEDICINE
paper.src: before penicillin (1940s), infected wounds were a leading cause of death

beats.text: The lights flicker. And at the end of the corridor stands a surgeon. Still in his mask.
He runs at you. You kick a gurney straight down the hall into him.
He goes down. He doesn't stay down. You don't wait to see more.
Your move. The pharmacy? Or the blood bank?
If you picked the blood bank, the smell of blood wakes up the whole ward. They come out of every room.
Ten doors. Ten of them. And you're standing in the middle of the hall.
If you picked the pharmacy, good move. Antibiotics, bandages, painkillers. You clean the cut, and you go.
The right way to treat a cut out here. Clean it with clean water. Press to stop the bleeding. Cover it. Change it every day.

paper.title: WOUND CARE
paper.src: basic first aid for minor cuts and scrapes

beats.text: Halfway. Five moves down. If you got all five right, you're already doing better than most of this city.

paper.title: HALFWAY CHECK
paper.src: keep count - your final score is at the end

beats.text: Noon. The mall. Every exit is chained shut, but the sports store is wide open.
You grab gloves, a helmet, and a bottle of water from a cooler that still feels cold.
Then the escalator starts moving. And it's full of them.
They tumble down the steps on top of each other. Twenty of them. And more behind.
A person can run about six miles an hour. On a bike, you can do fifteen.

paper.title: SPEED MATH
lines: THE DEAD: AS FAST AS YOU
paper.src: typical jogging and casual cycling speeds

beats.text: Your move. Grab a bike? Or a skateboard?
If you took the skateboard, the wheels catch on broken glass, and you go flying.
You hit the tile hard. And by the time you look up, they're already on you.
If you took the bike, good move. You ride it straight through the food court, and out the loading dock.
Behind you, the food court tables go flying as they chase. But on two wheels, you are gone.
The loading dock door is jammed halfway. You duck flat on the handlebars and slide right under it.
Three P.M. The streets are blocked, so you go up. Roof to roof.
From up here, you can see the whole city. Smoke in every direction. And one helicopter circling a tower downtown.
You clear one gap. Then another.
Twice, your foot slips on loose gravel. Twice, you catch yourself.
Then the next gap is twelve feet. With a bag on your back, you'll make eight. Maybe.
Your move. Jump it anyway? Or use the window cleaner's rope across the gap?
If you jumped, you hit the far wall, and you hang by your fingertips. Right above them.
Your fingers slip one at a time. And sixty feet below, they're waiting with their arms up.
If you took the rope, good move. Hand over hand, over sixty feet of nothing.
Your arms are shaking when you reach the other side. But you're across. And they're not.
Five P.M. The river bridge. The only way across. And it's packed. A thousand dead, shoulder to shoulder.
Cars bumper to bumper. And between them, every one of the dead is facing your way.
Your move. Push through on the bridge? Or jump into the river?
If you pushed through, you make it forty feet. Then hands grab your bag, and pull you down.
A thousand of them. One of you. The bridge was never a path. It was a trap.
If you jumped, good move. Feet first. Arms crossed. Body straight.
You hit the water like a pencil. It's so cold, it punches the air right out of your lungs.
Cold water has a rule. One minute to control your breathing. Ten minutes before your arms quit. One hour before you pass out.
You float. You breathe. And you let the current carry you to the far bank.
You crawl out on the far bank, soaked and freezing. Wet clothes pull heat out of your body way faster than air.
Water steals your body heat about twenty five times faster than air. So you wring out every layer, and you keep moving.

paper.title: WET = COLD
paper.src: water conducts heat roughly 25 times faster than air

beats.text: Behind you, on the bridge, a thousand heads watch you go. Not one of them follows you into the water.
Seven P.M. Searchlights. A military checkpoint. Soldiers checking everyone for bites.
A soldier with a megaphone. Hands where we can see them. One at a time.
You have a scratch on your arm. From the glass. Not a bite. But they can't know that.
The soldier's flashlight stops on your arm.
Your move. Tell them about the scratch? Or hide it?
If you hid it, they find it anyway. To them, hidden means bitten. The gate closes in your face.
Through the fence, you can see the tents, the lights, the hot food. And you're on the wrong side of it.
If you told them, good move. The medic checks it, cleans it, and waves you through.
Behind the fence, tents, lights, hot food. And a sign. Last helicopter, nine P.M.
You look at your watch. Eight fifty. You run.
Ten floors of stairs. Your legs are burning. Then the roof door.
Eight fifty nine P.M. The roof of the evacuation tower. The last helicopter is already lifting.
And the stairwell door bursts open behind you. Five hundred of them.
Your move. Jump for the ladder? Or wait for the next helicopter?
If you waited, there is no next one.
The sound of the rotors fades. And all five hundred of them turn to look at you.
If you jumped, good move. Your fingers close around the last rung. And the city falls away beneath you.
For one second, the ladder swings out over nothing but fire. You don't let go.
You made it.
Below you, the city goes dark, one block at a time. Twenty four hours. Ten moves. And you're still breathing.
Now count your moves. Ten out of ten, you're a legend. Seven or more, you survived. Under five, you'd be one of them.
Comment your score. And subscribe, because your next move is coming.
And tell me which move almost got you.
